analysis.one_liner: Taxes large investment funds 15% when they buy single-family homes and strips their landlord tax breaks.
analysis.headline: A 15% excise tax on hedge-fund purchases of single-family homes was proposed by a bipartisan Senate pair in February 2026, and the bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee with no action since introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge a 15% tax every time a large investment fund — defined as an entity managing at least $50 million in pooled investor money — buys a house or small residential building of 1 to 4 units. It would also take away the tax breaks those funds get as landlords: no deduction for mortgage interest or depreciation starting in 2031, no pass-through business deduction in 2036, and a 5-point higher corporate tax rate starting in 2036. The goal is to make it less profitable for Wall Street funds to buy up homes and outbid ordinary buyers.
analysis.who_benefits: Prospective homebuyers who compete against cash-rich investment funds at open houses, and renters in neighborhoods where large landlords own many single-family homes. If funds buy fewer homes, more houses stay available to owner-occupants, and any revenue raised goes to the Treasury for general use.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homebuyers and renters competing with investors

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 15% excise tax on the purchase price whenever a covered investment fund acquires a residential property of 1 to 4 dwelling units, raising the cost of the fund's bid on every house it buys.

The tax applies to any purchase made to rent out, flip, or hold, with an exception only when the property immediately becomes and stays the principal residence of a person with an ownership stake in the fund — so it targets investor purchases, not home ownership.

Strips the tax advantages that make corporate landlording more profitable: covered funds in the rental business would lose the mortgage interest deduction and depreciation deductions on single-family rentals starting in 2031, and the pass-through business income deduction in 2036.
Adds a 5-percentage-point corporate surtax on covered funds starting in 2036, and excludes nonprofits and homebuilders who build homes for sale, so new construction is not discouraged.

analysis.who_pays: Hedge funds, private equity firms, and REITs with $50 million or more in assets that buy or rent out single-family homes and small multifamily properties. They would pay 15% of the purchase price on each new acquisition and lose landlord tax deductions on their existing rental business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hedge funds and REITs owning rental homes

drawbacks.text: The tax applies only to homes purchased after the law takes effect, so it does nothing about the homes large investors already own — the existing stock of fund-owned rentals stays exactly where it is.

The covered group is narrow: only entities that manage pooled investor money, hold at least $50 million in assets, and act as fiduciaries. Other kinds of large corporate buyers of homes are not covered.

Removing mortgage interest and depreciation deductions raises the cost of operating rentals for large landlords, and some of that cost could be passed on to tenants as higher rent — the same renters the bill is meant to help.
The key provisions are phased in late: the deduction rollbacks start in 2031 and the corporate surtax and pass-through change not until 2036, so the effect on investor behavior would build slowly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The 15% purchase tax is a direct, understandable disincentive that would bite immediately on new investor acquisitions, which is the bill's strongest feature. But the bill is narrower than its framing: it leaves existing fund-owned homes untouched, exempts large buyers that don't fit the pooled-fund definition, delays the deduction rollbacks by years, and dedicates none of the revenue to affordable housing. The main risk — large landlords passing higher operating costs to tenants — is real but modest, since the purchase tax pushes funds out of buying homes rather than deep into the rental business.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late February 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no votes.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on February 26, 2026, with Senator Hawley joining as its one cosponsor — a Democrat-Republican pairing.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which handles all tax legislation.
No further action — no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the record since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large investment funds that buy and rent single-family homes are better off for now: their tax treatment is unchanged while the bill sits untouched in committee, and ordinary buyers continue to bid against them on equal terms for the funds.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its introduction in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the sole cosponsor, giving the bill a bipartisan sponsor pair.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and have taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Institutional single-family rental industry
against.role: Hedge funds, private equity firms, and REITs that own rental homes
against.what_they_did: Companies in this industry have a direct financial stake in the bill failing; large single-family landlords have historically lobbied against state and federal restrictions on investor home purchases.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsors are one Democrat and one Republican, and no votes have occurred, so the partisan shape of wider support is unknown.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity in single-family rentals
industries.note: These funds would pay 15% of the price on every home they buy and lose mortgage interest, depreciation, and pass-through deductions on their rental business. Their interest in this bill runs directly against buyers priced out of the market and tenants facing concentrated corporate landlords.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts (REITs) holding single-family homes
industries.note: REITs are explicitly included in the covered entities, so they face the same 15% acquisition tax and lost deductions. The bill would make buying single-family homes for rent materially less profitable for them.

Builders whose main business is constructing or rehabilitating homes for sale are exempted from the tax, and fewer institutional buyers competing for finished homes and lots works in their interest too.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate tax bills referred to the Finance Committee die there without a hearing, and this one has only two sponsors and no committee action more than a year before the Congress ends. Unless the committee chair schedules it or it gets attached to a larger tax package, it is likely to expire at the end of this Congress without a vote; the bipartisan sponsor pairing gives it a talking point but not the committee scheduling power it needs.
